pairs.titel: What did she promise the English?
pairs.frage: The letter dictated at Poitiers in March 1429, and what she told her judges two years later.
pairs.note: In 1429 she summons the king of England and his captains to go home 'or wait for news of the Maid', and promises that King Charles will enter Paris. On 1 March 1431, after the letter had been read to her and she had denied three of its phrases, she tells the court that within seven years the English will lose a greater pledge than Orléans and 'everything in France'. Paris opened to Charles VII in April 1436.

pairs.frage: The summons she dictated in March 1429, and what the city's Journal says the English did with it.
pairs.note: The letter offers the English peace if they leave France and promises them, if they do not, 'a tumult such as there has not been in France for a thousand years'. By the Journal's account the captains kept her herald, called her whore and cowgirl, and threatened to burn her; a month later they repeated the threat from the Tourelles. The Journal was compiled after Rouen, and its readers knew the end.

pairs.frage: Christine's prophecy of July 1429, and the letter sent to Bohemia in Jeanne's name eight months later.
pairs.note: Christine foretells that the Maid will destroy 'the heretics of filthy life' without mercy and then lead Charles to the Holy Land. The letter to the Hussites, composed by a clerk, threatens to leave the English and turn on Bohemia 'with the edge of the sword'. Neither happened. Fourteen months after the letter, the court at Rouen sentenced Jeanne herself as a heretic.

pairs.frage: The Burgundian chronicler's account of May 1430, and Jeanne's answer to her judges ten months later.
pairs.note: Monstrelet says the Maid 'had the head cut off' a valiant captain of his party after the fight near Lagny. At Rouen she said Franquet had confessed to being a murderer, thief and traitor, had been tried for fifteen days by the bailli of Senlis and the justice of Lagny, and that she had first tried to exchange him for a prisoner of her own; when that man died, she let justice take its course. Both agree that she could have saved him and did not. The judges listed it among the deeds they put to her as possible mortal sins.

pairs.titel: What did she say about the Church?
pairs.frage: Her answer in the prison session of 17 March 1431, and the twelfth article the judges drew from it.
pairs.note: In her prison Jeanne said that God and the Church were 'all one', that she submitted all her deeds to the Church above, and that on the Church Militant she would answer nothing more for now. The twelfth article turns this into a refusal to submit to 'any man in the world', made, it says, against the article of the creed explained to her many times. The Faculty of Decrees called it schism; the nullity trial asked whether the articles had fairly stated her answers.

pairs.frage: The schedule she signed on 24 May, and what she said of it four days later.
pairs.note: The schedule confesses that she 'feigned' her revelations, wore indecent clothing, desired bloodshed and was schismatic, and promises never to return to these errors; it is signed 'Jehanne' with a cross. On 28 May she says she never meant to revoke her voices, that she did not understand what was in the schedule, and that what she said she said for fear of the fire. The court read the second statement as relapse; the court of 1456 asked what she had been given to sign.

pairs.titel: What did she sign at Saint-Ouen?
pairs.frage: The abjuration entered in the record of 1431, and the usher who read her the schedule, twenty-five years later.
pairs.note: The record gives a long abjuration in French, confessing that she had feigned her revelations, worn indecent clothing, desired the shedding of blood and been schismatic, signed 'Jehanne' with a cross. Jean Massieu, who read the schedule aloud to her, told the nullity court that it was about eight lines long, forbade her arms, men's clothes and cropped hair, and was not the one in the record; that she asked for it to be seen by the Church first; and that Érard told her she would burn that day if she did not sign. The second trial rested much of its case on this difference.

pairs.frage: The church's sentence of 30 May 1431, and her confessor's account of what followed it.
pairs.note: The church court declares her a relapsed heretic, casts her out 'as a rotten limb' and leaves her to the secular power, asking it to temper its sentence. By Ladvenu's account the secular judges sat on their platform and passed no sentence at all: two sergeants led her down and handed her to the executioner. Isambart remembers only the words 'Do your duty.' Each court left the death to the other; the nullity trial counted it among the faults of the first.
